item.title: 'You should be ashamed of yourself': Heated Senate debates become personal
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WCSH Candidates faced off in heated debates Thursday night in two of the country’s most competitive Senate races , showing how bitter — and personal — each contest has become. In Maine, Democratic nominee Troy Jackson told GOP Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” after she suggested a protester was one of his supporters. And in Alaska, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan questioned Democratic opponent Mary Peltola’s “character” while citing allegations she mistreated staff. “I think that Alaskans have had it up to here with the lying and dishonesty,” Peltola said during another exchange. “Dan, you should be ashamed of yourself.” The races are unfolding thousands of miles apart but both critical to the Senate majority. Collins, a moderate Republican, is seeking reelection in a blue state, while Sullivan is running for another term in more GOP-leaning Alaska where Peltola, a former congresswoman, is well-known. Both debates showed how much of a political liability President Donald Trump’s war in Iran has become for Republican incumbents. Sullivan said it “needs to end soon,” while Collins continued to insist Trump should have consulted Congress on the conflict. Here’s a look at key moments from the debates. US Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic candidate for the US Senate Troy Jackson are seen during their debate at the Gracie Theatre in Bangor, Maine on Thursday. - Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images A protester disrupts Collins on data centers The fourth and final Senate debate in Maine grew heated as Collins and Jackson sharpened their attacks. Within minutes, a protester shouted at Collins about the impact of data centers, forcing the debate to a brief halt. “AI data centers are destroying our climate. They are poisoning our waters,” the protester yelled. Following the incident, Collins said the protester “is obviously one of Troy’s supporters.” “Oh, shut up,” Jackson replied, saying he did not know who the person was. unknown content item - Corruption allegations and campaign financing in Maine During the Collins-Jackson debate, both candidates tried to portray their opponent as corrupt, a major theme that has loomed over the hotly contested race and the midterms nationally. Collins cornered Jackson for not sharing his FEC report with her on Wednesday, a promise he made at their debate earlier this week. Jackson said he missed his self-imposed deadline because it took longer to process the donations from 200,000 people to his campaign than he expected. “I had to make sure this report was right. It was my first one,” Jackson said. Throughout the campaign, Jackson has framed Collins as being influenced by her donors and touted that he doesn’t take any corporate PAC money. Collins tried to flip the script on Thursday by dinging Jackson for running joint ads with his party’s Senate campaign arm, which does take money from corporations, and for not disclosing his donors. Jackson said he did not control their donations to the Senate campaign committee but did concede his campaign has taken money from billionaires. “That is accurate. But I haven’t made any deals like Senator Collins has with those billionaires. I don’t owe them any votes. I am going to tax those billionaires when I get to the US Senate. So, if they want to give me money during this campaign, I guess that’s up to them,” Jackson said. When it was Jackson’s turn to ask Collins a question, he got personal. In defending his credentials and pushing back on Collins’ critique that he doesn’t have the right experience, Jackson exclaimed, “Is it just me that you look down on or is it working-class people overall?” Collins further distances from Trump on Iran war Collins doubled down on her criticism of the Iran war as the Maine Republican continues to distance herself from Trump. When asked if Congress should have been consulted before Trump decided to go to war, Collins said, “Congress definitely should have been consulted.” But Collins added that that the War Powers Resolution gave Trump the flexibility to act unilaterally within the first 60 days of the conflict, which she said is why she did not start voting to rein in Trump’s war powers until after those initial 60 days had passed. unknown content item - Iran war’s consequences also hangs over Alaska debate Sullivan repeatedly had to grapple with issues where Trump has not made the race easy for him. The war in Iran, for example, has led to especially high fuel costs in Alaska. Sullivan said he has opposed limiting Trump’s Iran powers because he supports the overall goal of preventing the country from obtaining a nuclear weapon. But he said the war “needs to end soon.” “The energy costs from this war are too high, but … the best way to bring down costs with regard to energy in Alaska is to produce more energy by and for Alaskans,” Sullivan said, suggesting Peltola could not be trusted to support that. Peltola blamed Washington politicians for “waging forever wars that are skyrocketing our costs.” And she scoffed at Sullivan’s pivot to the topic of domestic energy production. “I have been a strong supporter of drilling in Alaska,” she said. “That is not the issue here.” Sullivan continued to show daylight with Trump when asked about Trump’s plan to buy Russian diesel . He reiterated his opposition, saying, “I don’t think it’s a good ideal at all,” and noting he “just led the effort” to pass new sanctions on Russia in Congress. Sullivan, Peltola spar over her treatment of staff Sullivan and Peltola clashed twice over a September story from The New York Times that alleged staff mistreatment by Peltola. In the article, her campaign pushed back on the suggestion she regularly abused her staff but said she occasionally “struggled to deal with her grief” after her mother and husband died in 2023. “I do not think that this election is about me on my worst day, and I found so many of these allegations concerning and outright fabrications or mass exaggerations of the truth,” Peltola said at the debate when asked about the Times report. Sullivan emphasized that the story was based on interviews with nine former staff members and at least 20 other people. “It’s not Mary Peltola on her worst day,” Sullivan said. “It’s Mary Peltola over the course of a couple years with dozens of people weighing in on this.” Sullivan brought up the Times story on his own earlier in the debate, saying Peltola has “treated young Alaskans horribly” and that it was “a character flaw.” Peltola called it “gossip” and “unfounded allegations” as Sullivan talked over her. “It’s the New York Times,” he said. “Read the article.” Sullivan questions whether Peltola got questions in advance The Times story was not the only cause for animosity between the two candidates. After Peltola criticized Sullivan about the war in Iran, looking down at notes on her podium as she spoke, Sullivan turned to the moderators. “We weren’t supposed to get these questions beforehand were, we?” he asked. “No, sir,” one moderator said before another added: “Neither one of you got questions beforehand. Absolutely not.” “OK,” Sullivan said. “I’m just watching my opponent read from questions that seem to be answered.” “I’m prepared,” Peltola said. Sullivan appeared to back down from his suggestion while speaking with reporters after the debate, according to Alaska Public Media , which quoted him telling the hosts, “I’m not blaming you guys.” This story has been updated with additional information. item.title: The U.S. economy is facing 2 hot wars heating up at a bad time for the White House
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Yields are above multidecade highs , both gas and diesel prices continue to climb , and critical midterm elections are around the corner. Adding to pressure on the US economy and the current administration, the world's two largest hot wars are heating up. 'Iran knows when the midterms are too' In the Middle East, dual fronts along the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea have seen a resurgence of conflict in recent weeks that has heavily disrupted oil flows in the region. (Yasin Demirci/Anadolu via Getty Images) Anadolu via Getty Images Multiple tankers and container ships in the Strait of Hormuz either caught fire or sank this week in the Iran-dominated waterway. The Washington Institute has tracked more than two dozen attacks recorded since the start of the month. President Trump has said the US military won't resume airstrikes inside Iran before the midterm elections as White House negotiators continue angling for a diplomatic solution to the conflict now in its eighth month. Read more: How to protect your money as Mideast turmoil fuels market volatility Middle Eastern crude oil and petroleum product exports have declined significantly over the past week. (Murat Usubali/Anadolu via Getty Images) Anadolu via Getty Images At the same time, administration officials are reportedly war-gaming a major offensive to come after the November elections, when the president will be less encumbered by the political needs of the Republican Party. "The Trump Administration does not want Brent crude oil at $106/bbl going into the midterm elections, just a month away, and has said that he only plans to escalate offenses against Iran after the midterms are over, with what he hopes to be, a red wave," Rabobank cross-asset macro strategist Molly Schwartz said in a recent note to clients. To the west along the Red Sea, Yemen's Houthi militants have sharply escalated their campaign against the Saudi coalition opposing the group's bid for wider territorial control, launching multiple rounds of strikes on major airports inside the kingdom that have killed more than a dozen people and wounded hundreds. Houthi militants recently struck an office building belonging to the state-managed oil giant Saudi Aramco ( 2223.SR ). While the kingdom's oil production remains largely undisrupted, violent pestering by the Iran-allied Houthis is driving up oil prices . Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on Oct. 3, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images) - via Getty Images "Iran knows when the midterms are too," Schwartz added, "and if they want to further complicate Trump's plans, now is the perfect time to have the Houthis stir up trouble and make it increasingly difficult for the US to avoid intervening." Ukraine, Russia, and Starlink throttling Ukraine and Russia, which have been at war since Russia executed a stealth annexation of Crimea in 2014 and invaded its neighbor in February 2022, recently both escalated offensive strikes against critical infrastructure ahead of another winter. Kyiv leverages long-range drone attacks to knock out oil refineries inside Russia, claiming to have disrupted half the country's refining capacity, while Moscow has repeatedly targeted power plants and other civilian infrastructure inside Ukraine. Over the weekend, President Trump called for an "energy ceasefire," part of a bid to bring down US diesel prices that has included a deal that will see the US buy Russian fuel , breaking with several years of sanctions meant to pressure the Kremlin's war chest. Plumes of smoke rise from fires at an oil refinery in Moscow following what the authorities said is a Ukrainian drone strike in the course of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, on Sept., 20, 2026. (Reuters/Stringer/File Photo) Reuters / REUTERS Shortly after the announcement, Russia launched a round of strikes against power plants in Ukraine, prompting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to say Kyiv would continue to target Russian refineries. On Wednesday, Ukraine reported rate-throttling of Starlink , satellite communications services developed by SpaceX ( SPCX ), and its military subscription service StarShield. On Thursday evening, citing an official familiar with the matter, Reuters reported that "the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House." Ukrainian troops use both Starlink and Starshield terminals. (ISW) Oil prices and yields pressure US economy Taken together, the conflicts are putting immense pressure on the global energy system — and, increasingly, on the US economy. While oil exports from the Persian Gulf have returned to prewar levels via alternative routes, exports through the waterway itself — which before the war accounted for roughly one-fifth of global oil flows — have remained far below prewar levels. And prior to 2022, Russia provided roughly 10% of the world's diesel exports. But Moscow has largely been cut off from the market after international sanctions and domestic export bans. The US economy is feeling the disruption: Yields on US 10-year and 30-year Treasurys have climbed to levels not seen since the early 2000s, pressuring consumer and corporate borrowers. Gasoline and diesel prices have soared to record levels. Wednesday marked a record for the number of days in a year that gasoline stayed above $4 per gallon. Recent reports from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed inflation readings on both consumer and producer prices accelerating faster than expected , with energy prices rising at the quickest pace since March, just after the start of the Iran war. For the White House, those economic pressures have complicated the outlook for midterm elections less than three weeks away. In comments to reporters on Wednesday night, President Trump said again that the war in Iran will "end very soon," and the White House is reportedly considering the use of a GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB) — the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal, which would mark a major step-up in escalation. President Trump speaks in the Rose Garden at the White House, Washington, D.C., on Oct. 15, 2026. (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images) JIM WATSON via Getty Images Iran is not backing down : Parliamentary speaker Mohamed Bagher Ghalibaf said on Wednesday that Iran will fight until its demands are met in negotiations. In Ukraine, President Zelensky has ordered renewed attacks on Russian refineries . And with only a few short weeks left until the midterms, the reheating of both wars has left the White House — and, by proxy, the US economy — between a rock and a hard place. item.title: Trump pauses Russia sanctions passed by Congress, citing U.S. national interest
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest. Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. It drew shift condemnation from congressional Democrats. Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham , the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine . Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia. An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president's handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump's approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress after midterm elections on Nov. 3. Sanctions were seen as part of Graham's legacy Graham, a close ally and friend of the president, had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July. He had advocated for stricter U.S. sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine. His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation — then changed his mind Friday. The package had been meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbor more than four years ago. The bill, also drafted by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving. It also directed Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. Blumenthal said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies.” “These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said. Democratic Virginia Rep. Don Beyer noted on social media shortly after the announcement of the sanctions being suspended that he and others had “warned" Trump might make such a move. The veteran congressman, who spoke out against the bill as it was debated, called on Congress to “fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine.” The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest. The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress. Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting. The Trump administration, meanwhile, had remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large majorities in the House and Senate following Graham’s sudden death — with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy. Trump's action follows announced diesel deal with Putin Under last week's agreement, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Trump’s striking a diesel deal with Putin has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine -- without making a different to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war on Iran. The sanctions that Trump has now suspended, meanwhile, also had become a campaign centerpiece for Sen. Darline Graham , the late senator’s sister who was appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term. She is now running to replace him in the Senate more permanently. Darline Graham said in a statement after Trump signed the bill, “I wish Lindsey were here to celebrate this historic day." In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham — who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week — said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed. She acknowledged, however, that it was the president’s purview as to how he implemented it. “It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia. “So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-puts-russia-sanctions-passed-014202867.html

item.title: DOJ warns California election officials of possible prosecution over noncitizen votes
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is escalating its fight with California ahead of next month's midterm election, warning that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution. The letter Friday from a senior Justice Department official and obtained first by The Associated Press is the latest salvo in an ongoing tussle with heavily Democratic California, coming just a day after the Trump administration sued the state to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. “The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful,” warns the letter from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department. It adds: “If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.” The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel's office and also is copied to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice. In response to the letter, Logan said his office is focused on conducting a fair and secure election while noting that Election Day is a mere 18 days away. “The U.S. Department of Justice has chosen to litigate their unverified assertions of voting eligibility. At this point, it is best for this to be addressed in court,” he said. The other offices and the state attorney general did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It is unclear how many individuals the Justice Department might look to try to investigate and charge, though any federal criminal cases in the Los Angeles area would be handled by the office of Bill Essayli, the region's top federal prosecutor and one of the Justice Department officials who filed the federal complaint Thursday against California. Trump weighed in late Friday, sharing on Truth Social a link to a news story about the letter and adding: “They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!” The Trump administration has made the pursuit of noncitizen voters a priority Sent less than three weeks before the Nov. 3 election, the letter adds to simmering tensions over voter rolls between California and the Justice Department and reflects the Trump administration's aggressive hunt for noncitizen voters . It has made the issue a priority this year, including by demanding detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens . There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state. That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero. That experience is backed up by research and investigations in various states, which make clear that voting by noncitizens is extremely rare. The letter follows a Justice Department lawsuit The Justice Department lawsuit was filed after California officials were given , and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. Rick Hasen, a UCLA law professor, said the letter “ups the ante by threatening election officials with potential criminal prosecution.” “It is deplorable that rather than work cooperatively and assist states in their election administration responsibilities, the federal government is making escalating threats and unreasonable demands beyond its power in the middle of an ongoing election,” he said. Justin Levitt, a former deputy assistant attorney general who teaches at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, dismissed the idea that an attempted prosecution of an election official using the letter’s rationale would hold up. “Courts haven’t been buying what DOJ has been selling, and nothing in this letter is calibrated to change course,” he said. “Fortunately, election officials — not just in Los Angeles, but across the country — are equipped to stand up to aggressive bullying. And the law is on their side.” Over 23 million people are registered statewide, and a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts could determine which party controls the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term. The Trump administration's escalating threats against California come as Democratic lawmakers are urging the Justice Department to honor its longstanding policy of not interfering in U.S. elections. Earlier Friday, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Dick Durbin, D-Il., wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified. ___ Associated Press writers Michael R. Blood in Los Angeles and Ali Swenson in New York contributed to this report. item.title: Trump's drug company holdings surged from $1.7 million to $56 million, Democrats say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Investments in pharmaceutical companies made on behalf of President Donald Trump increased significantly after he returned to the White House last year, with his portfolio adding millions of dollars in stock in firms that benefited from a Republican-backed law that shields certain medications from Medicare price negotiations, according to a report from congressional Democrats. The report, released Friday by the Joint Economic Committee’s minority arm, found that Trump’s pharmaceutical stock holdings grew from a maximum reported value of $1.7 million in 2024 to as much as $56.2 million at the end of 2025. The report said that included up to $39.1 million worth of stock held in companies that benefited from exemptions to Medicare’s drug price negotiation program, which came through a provision in Republicans' 2025 tax and spending law . Additional analysis of Trump's financial disclosures provided by committee Democrats showed that his investment portfolio bought as much as $2.55 million in shares of pharmaceutical companies benefiting from the exemptions on three dates before he signed the legislation in July 2025. That included up to $950,000 in purchases on July 1, 2025, the day the Senate passed the bill . His portfolio also bought as much as $1 million in AbbVie stock in August 2025, after the bill became law. The Republican president’s wealth has grown since he took office last year through a web of business interests , many of which have benefited from the policy moves of his administration. The White House has repeatedly denied any ethics issues and accused Democrats of “attempts to fabricate conflicts of interest.” The report also noted that the exemptions policy could leave some Medicare beneficiaries paying thousands of dollars more for certain cancer treatments and other medications than they would have if Medicare had been allowed to negotiate lower prices. The findings come as Trump has made lowering prescription drug costs a central part of his healthcare policy, striking deals with pharmaceutical companies that his administration says will make medications more affordable for Americans, although drug pricing is based on a complicated set of factors . Recent polling from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that most Americans think Trump is profiting off the presidency in unethical or illegal ways and is focused more on his wealth than on helping people like them. Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan, who leads the Joint Economic Committee’s minority arm, called the report’s findings “outrageous and yet typical from this president, who makes the American people foot the bill again and again for his own gains.” Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. He denied any conflict of interest. “Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold,” Ingle said in a statement. A law from President Joe Biden's Democratic administration allowed Medicare for the first time to negotiate prices for some of the costliest prescription drugs. Republicans' 2025 tax and spending bill expanded an existing exemption for medications developed to treat rare diseases or conditions, delaying when certain costly drugs could become eligible for negotiations or excluding them entirely, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF. Also known as the orphan drug exclusion, the carveout allows drug companies to continue charging lucrative prices that might otherwise have been reduced through Medicare negotiations. Supporters of the change argued that a broader exemption would encourage drug companies to develop treatments for rare diseases. Critics say it allows makers of blockbuster medications to avoid negotiations that could lower costs for Medicare and its recipients. The report estimated that Medicare beneficiaries receiving the cancer drugs Keytruda, manufactured by Merck, and Opdivo, by Bristol Myers Squibb, could pay roughly $5,000 more annually than they would if Medicare negotiated prices for the medications. Trump's portfolio includes stock in both firms. The report also said that Trump's portfolio continued to buy and sell pharma company stocks throughout the first eight months of 2026, adding as much as $3.5 million in stock wealth in the sector. All recent U.S. presidents have dumped their stocks before assuming office, put their money in broadly diversified funds or set up a “blind” trust so they couldn’t even know what they owned. Trump has put his broader business interests in a trust managed by his sons. But the arrangement rejects the conflict of interest protections that his recent predecessors in office had instituted. ___ Associated Press writer Bernard Condon in New York contributed to this report. item.title: Amber Guyger released on parole after serving 7 years for Botham Jean’s murder
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Former Dallas police Officer Amber Guyger (left) was sentenced to 10 years in prison for the 2018 shooting death of Botham Jean. (Archive Photos) Former Dallas police Officer Amber Guyger walked free from prison Friday morning after serving seven years behind bars for the murder of Botham Jean. Guyger, 38, shot 26-year-old Jean inside his apartment in September 2018. He had been sitting on his couch eating ice cream when Guyger, who was off-duty but still in uniform, opened the door. She said she mistook Jean’s apartment for her own and believed he was a burglar. He lived on the fourth floor; she lived on the third. She was found guilty of murder and sentenced to 10 years in prison, but was granted parole earlier this month. Guyger was released after 10 a.m. from the Christina Melton Crain Unit in Gatesville. CBS reported live from the unit, but news cameras didn’t capture her release. Texas Department of Criminal Justice officials said Guyger was released into community supervision. Guyger was required to travel directly to her new residence and check in immediately with her parole officer, according to Texas parole requirements . She was allowed to take home personal items accumulated while in prison and will either wear state-issued civilian clothes or clothes brought to her by visitors or the people picking her up. Guyger walked out with her parole papers, a temporary ID and a prepaid debit card or check for money left in her inmate trust account. Guyger was denied parole in 2024 after the state parole board said she was not rehabilitated or ready for release. Her request was granted this time after a review found her record showed no documented pattern of violence, that she maintained a “satisfactory institutional adjustment” and that she completed a treatment plan that “should enhance” her chances of obtaining — and keeping — a full-time job, a Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles spokesperson said in early October. The board has several options for what type of parole to grant an inmate, a vote that depends on individual circumstances and the inmate’s behavior during time served. Guyger was granted direct release with no additional restrictions beyond her parole conditions, the least restrictive form of parole approval a Texas inmate can receive. The decision to release her sparked a new wave of interest and emotion around the case, which drew international attention, sparked protests and led Texas lawmakers to pass the Botham Jean Act. Also known as Bo’s Law, the statute requires officers to keep their body cameras on for the entirety of their participation in an investigation. That same year, Dallas renamed part of South Lamar Street for Jean. “The past eight years have been an incredibly traumatic and painful experience for Botham Jean’s family,” the family said in an official statement released in early October. “The loss of Botham has left our family forever dismembered, and that is something we continue to live with every day.” A large photo of Botham Jean is displayed with photos and cards on one of the tables in his childhood home in Castries, St. Lucia on Sept. 25, 2018. Botham Jean was shot and killed in his apartment by off-duty Dallas police Officer Amber Guyger. (Vernon Bryant/Staff Photographer) Guyger’s parole conditions were not released, but her trial attorney, who no longer represents her, told The Dallas Morning News after the parole vote that she has a job that will keep her out of the public life and a living arrangement that will stay private. “She’s hopeful, optimistic, tremendously remorseful,” attorney Robert Rogers said. “That’s probably something she’ll always live with.” Parole conditions Most parolees must follow the same basic set of rules, alongside any special conditions decided by the parole board, which are typically kept confidential. Guyger will have to follow her parole conditions until September 2029. Failure to follow the conditions can result in parole revocation, which sends the inmate back to prison for the remainder of their sentence, or lesser sanctions such as curfew adjustments or brief incarceration in a facility designed for parolees. State law requires all parolees to get permission from their parole officer if they want to change residences or leave the state. They must be working or in school, and they have to check in regularly with their parole officer, submit monthly education or work reports, and submit to random alcohol and drug testing and unannounced searches. They’re forbidden from breaking the law, owning or being around firearms and ammunition, and from contacting the victim directly or indirectly. They must make restitution payments and reimburse the prison for some educational programs. Guyger still faces a judgment of nearly $100 million from a federal civil suit connected to Jean’s murder. Immigrant advocacy groups representing migrant children have sued the Trump administration to stop what they call a "cruel and unlawful scheme" to fast-track migrant children's asylum cases. In a complaint filed Thursday night, the groups allege that new government policies have transformed the asylum process for migrant children into a "deportation assembly line depriving them of their rights." The lawsuit comes as immigration attorneys and advocates say unaccompanied migrant children are being rushed through the immigration system and that their deportations have been accelerated as part of the Trump administration's aggressive immigration crackdown . Trump administration offering migrant children $3,000 to self-deport "A system that moves faster and that is by design made so that children are unable to access lawyers and are railroaded into deportation orders is not justice. It's assembly line deportation of the most vulnerable among us," said Lindsay Toczylowski, co-founder of the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, during a press call. The groups said unaccompanied children are facing rushed hearings, difficulty finding lawyers, and accelerated removal orders, including in cases involving alleged human trafficking and threats of violence. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News. In the suit, the groups said that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has changed practices through a series of recent policy shifts that include reducing notice times for asylum interviews -- in some cases proving less than 24 hours' notice. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images, FILE - PHOTO: In this Oct. 15, 2025, file photo, a family walks past federal agents as they arrive for their court hearing in immigration court at the Jacob K. Javits Federal Building in New York. In the complaint, the groups also said that the Department of Justice has instructed immigration judges to complete all removal proceedings for detained unaccompanied children by Jan. 31, 2027. The suit comes two days after the Department of Homeland Security announced it was offering unaccompanied migrant children $3,000 to self-deport , a $500 increase over last year's incentive. Earlier this month, the federal government quietly assembled a team of government attorneys to represent migrant children in court after the administration cut ties with a number of immigration advocacy groups that had previously provided those services. item.title: Trump officials scrutinized Omar in 2019. They didn't find citizenship issues.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Seven years ago, a political appointee in the first Trump administration approached U.S. immigration authorities with a request that alarmed career staffers: Scrub the immigration records of Rep. Ilhan Omar, then a newly elected Democratic lawmaker from Minnesota, for evidence of fraud. That 2019 demand, detailed by three former immigration officials, struck staffers at the time as a highly unusual effort to wield federal power to dig up compromising material on a sitting member of Congress who was a prominent critic of President Donald Trump. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The request sparked a swift review examining Omar’s history, her family’s past as Somali refugees resettled in the United States and rumors that had circulated for years in conservative media over her marriage. Homeland Security Investigations - the investigative arm of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement - ultimately determined there was insufficient evidence of wrongdoing, one of the former officials said. The idea of pursuing a full investigation was eventually abandoned. Now, though, with Trump back in the White House and his administration using federal power to take aim at perceived enemies, Omar has once again found herself in federal crosshairs. She is now facing an inquiry over some of the same allegations investigators previously deemed not worth pursuing. The current effort - which burst into public view Monday as federal agents descended upon Omar’s D.C. home - is focused on whether she or her father lied on paperwork they submitted to obtain legal status and eventual citizenship after arriving in the U.S. in the 1990s. Investigators are reexamining questions about Omar’s birth date and her late father’s past military history in Somalia, which had passed scrutiny during the 2019 review. Depending on their findings, the administration could seek to charge Omar with a crime or move to challenge her status in the country. But such a step would be a sharp reversal of the earlier review, which found no issue with her naturalization, one of the former officials familiar with the earlier effort said. “I think her citizenship is solid and there wasn’t any fraud there,” the ex-official said. Omar has dismissed the revived investigation as yet another example of the Justice Department, under Trump, attempting “to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” “Trump has spread lie after lie about the Congresswoman in a desperate attempt to justify his extraordinary abuse of power,” her spokesperson said in a statement Thursday. “This is politically motivated and an escalation of Trump’s personal vendetta against her lasting over a decade.” This account of the Trump administration’s current and past efforts to investigate and possibly build a case against Omar is based on interviews with a dozen people, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss nonpublic details of those probes. Several current and former officials raised questions about the scope, tactics and motivations driving the current Omar investigation, which they say appears to be disregarding key norms on how immigration reviews are typically handled and bypassing guardrails intended to ensure federal inquiries, including those looking into sitting lawmakers, are not perceived to be driven by politics. A spokesperson for the Justice Department said the agency does not comment on ongoing investigations. The Department of Homeland Security referred questions to the Justice Department. Questions about the probe came into play ahead of this week’s highly public search of Omar’s home. Before carrying out the search, prosecutors spent days working to allay concerns from a federal judge that their plans could run afoul of constitutional protections shielding members of Congress from unwarranted executive branch intrusion, according to three people familiar with the matter. U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew J. Sharbaugh, who ultimately signed off on the warrant, first imposed strict conditions on how the search should be carried out, the people said. His limits on the search appeared intended to ensure that the warrant fell in line with the D.C. court’s interpretation of the Constitution’s speech and debate clause, which generally shields lawmakers’ legislative duties and actions from criminal probes. As part of the search, agents removed boxes of documents and seized Omar’s cellphone and passport, one person familiar with the matter said. Trump has assailed Omar for years, and this week condemned her again on social media and public remarks. “I think she’s a terrible person,” he told reporters. “But that’s really up to the DOJ. I have nothing to do with it.” Trump’s administration has also made clear its scrutiny on Omar is not limited to immigration issues. Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney in D.C., announced Tuesday her office had launched its own investigation into Omar’s personal finances, tied to disclosure statements she filed in Congress last year and separate from the immigration probe. Pirro, a former Fox News host, once drew a highly unusual public rebuke from the network in 2019 for on-air comments suggesting that Omar, as a Muslim, could not be loyal to the U.S. Constitution. Omar’s office has previously dismissed questions raised by House Republicans over her financial disclosure statements as a right-wing attempt to “manufacture controversy.” However, federal prosecutors’ interest in the finances of Omar extend back to the Biden administration, according to two people familiar with the effort. Those individuals said it was not clear why the investigation during the prior administration appeared to have stalled. But the revived immigration investigation into Omar appears to be the furthest along and the administration’s higher priority. Alessandra P. Serano, an associate deputy attorney general who is playing a key role in the probe, went before the judge seeking the search warrant for Omar’s home, two people familiar with the matter said. Attorney General Todd Blanche also recently dispatched Serano, a trusted aide, to Florida to check in on the high-profile and struggling Florida-based investigation into former Obama and Biden-era officials, according to multiple people. Authorities have issued more than a dozen subpoenas related to Omar and the investigation into her, including some to her siblings, seeking testimony before a grand jury in Minneapolis in the coming weeks, two people said. The Washington Post has reported that investigators are focused on whether Omar or her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, intentionally misstated her birth date on immigration paperwork so she could be eligible to derive citizenship through him as a minor when he was naturalized in 2000. Investigators are also scrutinizing whether Omar’s father may have purposefully lied or omitted information on his past military service in Somalia that could have made him ineligible to obtain legal status in the country. But three former officials involved in the 2019 review of Omar’s immigration file said both of those issues were considered during that inquiry. An official with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, who was normally tasked with scrutinizing the backgrounds of people including serious criminals, terrorists and potential national security threats, was asked in 2019 to review Omar’s background. The then-freshman lawmaker had emerged as a frequent focus of conservative attacks. At the time, the agency was primarily focused on possible fraud related to Omar’s marriage to her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. Right-wing commentators had repeatedly pressed unsubstantiated claims that Omar and Elmi were siblings who carried out a sham marriage so that Elmi could obtain U.S. immigration benefits. Elmi had previously filed an immigration petition related to his marriage-based green card that would move it from conditional status to permanent. USCIS requested additional evidence due to concerns over the validity of his marriage, but Elmi withdrew the application following that request, one of the former officials said. Elmi could not immediately be reached for comment Thursday. The 2019 review of Omar also looked at other issues, some of which are being examined anew. For instance, back then, USCIS quickly determined it could not accurately answer questions over Omar’s age because refugees frequently come from countries with little or no birth records, making it hard to determine with any certainty. “That’s not strange and that’s not a red flag to me,” one of the former officials said. “It’s just very, very common that there aren’t great birth records.” The agency also examined Omar’s father’s immigration file but did not find any issues, according to the former official. The USCIS officer tasked with vetting Omar produced a memo of those findings and shared it with a senior USCIS official and a fraud detention official before the effort was ultimately abandoned, the person said. Due to the sensitivity, the memo was printed out, and distributed in person, and not shared over email. Whether the current investigation will uncover more substantial evidence to back the administration’s fraud claims remains to be seen. Even if the Trump administration finds wrongdoing, any attempt to strip her citizenship would likely be lengthy and result in a legal battle. The administration, however, is also exploring the possibility that it could seek to revoke her citizenship certificate if the current investigation does not result in criminal charges or a conviction, a senior Trump administration official said. Revocation is a rarely employed USCIS administrative process that can be used to cancel the document due to fraud or an error. The process is not restricted to a certain period of time like criminal denaturalizations, which are subject to a 10-year statute of limitations. The revocation would not remove her citizenship but would make it challenging to obtain some government documents. This action could open the door to immigration-related charges and possibly removal proceedings, though such a novel application of the administrative authority would almost certainly face challenges from Omar in court. In a statement, Omar’s spokesperson assailed the Trump administration’s efforts to target the congresswoman. “He has lied about her family, about her immigration history, and about her love of this country,” the statement read. “But the truth is that Trump’s push to strip her of her citizenship and deport her has no basis in the law and has no precedent. This isn’t a legitimate law enforcement action.” Alexei Koseff contributed to this report. CORRECTION: A previous version of this article incorrectly described the length of a memo a USCIS officer produced about Rep. Ilhan Omar. The memo was several pages, not one page. President Trump’s embattled new press secretary Katie Zacharia was forced out Friday after less than a week on the job. “It was an honor to work for him,” Zacharia wrote on social media , confirming widespread reports that Trump had let her go. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung told CNN in a statement that Zacharia “will continue to support the President as she transitions to a new role.” Zacharia is the shortest-tenured White House press secretary in U.S. history. Earlier Friday, Trump signaled that Zacharia was on her way out, telling reporters that he had asked Zacharia to "reconsider" whether she "need[s] this." "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy and I don't think you could ever be happy in this job,'" Trump said. Asked if he was planning to "fire" Zacharia, the president said no. But, he added, "I want her to have a good life. I don't want [her] to have a life like she's led in the last three days. She is being brutalized by the media." Around the same time, multiple outlets reported that Zacharia had already been let go. Citing "three people familiar with the matter," the New York Times reported on Friday afternoon that Trump had "fired" Zacharia. A senior White House official told Fox News that Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role, and CBS News, Politico and the Washington Post published similar reports. Trump: "I told Katie that in my opinion she was treated very very unfairly by the news. Let's call it the fake news. I said, 'Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this.' We're talking about doing something. I want her to have a good life. She's being brutalized by the… pic.twitter.com/Ivkk5imCjS — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 16, 2026 The president announced on Friday, Oct. 9, that he had chosen Zacharia, a conservative commentator and former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration in August. Zacharia started at the White House on Monday gave her first press briefing on Tuesday. But she has spent the days since then facing questions about her own legal credentials rather than Trump's agenda. In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump described Zacharia as an "attorney" as well as "a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" Zacharia holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, and her LinkedIn page says she served as "general counsel" at Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former acting Kennedy Center director Ric Grenell to promote conservative policies in the Golden State. In media appearances, Zacharia has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer. But the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that while Zacharia sat for the California bar exam after graduating from law school, she "didn't pass." A senior administration official confirmed to NBC News that Zacharia did not pass the California bar exam. Reuters also investigated her credentials and "could not find records showing Zacharia was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any U.S. state or the District of Columbia." Asked by reporters Tuesday on the South Lawn where she passed the bar, Zacharia twice replied, "When I moved to China." In a phone interview with the New York Times on Wednesday , Zacharia said she misheard the question. "I assumed the question was, 'Where were you after law school?'" she told the paper. "That's all I could hear over the sound of Marine One. And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question." Zacharia pointed out that it was only her second day on the job. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia looks on as President Trump speaks to reporters on the South Lawn on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson In a statement to the Washington Post , the White House said that "Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law." According to USA Today , Zacharia "worked for a Chinese law firm's international-practice team on multimillion-dollar shareholder agreements involving investments through the World Bank." She did not attempt to take the bar exam a second time. On Thursday, Zacharia confimed that she did not pass the bar, telling the conservative outlet Real America's Voice that she was "incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited" at the time by her impending marriage and move to China. "We just said… 'I'll take the bar and see what happens,'" Zacharia recalled. "The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China." On Wednesday, a nonprofit watchdog group called Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the California bar asking it to investigate whether Zacharia had violated state law by "repeatedly holding herself out as a lawyer." White House spokesperson Steven Cheung responded on social media by dismissing the Campaign for Accountability as a "radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome." Legal experts told the Times that it's debatable whether a law school graduate can describe herself as a "lawyer" before she passes the bar. But she cannot call herself an "attorney" — someone who is licensed to practice law and give legal advice — nor can she serve as a "general counsel" or as an "associate" at a Chinese law firm, they added. Zacharia told Real America's Voice that she was "very careful about how I executed this and I never came across as somebody who was an attorney-at-law." "I consulted for a very long time many people in the field — 'Is it OK and acceptable if I label myself 'lawyer' … and provide legal analysis, not legal advice," she explained. "They said, 'Absolutely,' across the board. 'You can call yourself a lawyer.'" On Thursday night, Fox News host Sean Hannity pressed Zacharia on her halting explanation . item.title: Oregon school shooter identified as 16-year-old former student
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A teacher and one of the three children who were killed in Thursday's mass shooting at a Bend, Ore., elementary school were identified on Friday during a press conference in which authorities provided additional details about the incident. The 16-year-old suspect, who was killed by a community member within minutes of opening fire at the school, was also identified. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said Friday that Rhoam Summer, a 5-year-old student, and Meghan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher, were among the four victims in a special education classroom at Silver Rail Elementary School. In a statement, Lambert's family described her as a native central Oregonian who grew up in Bend and had a passion for playing sports, especially volleyball. "Her goal was to be an educator and teach in the school district she loved growing up in," the statement continued. "Silver Rail was her first job as a teacher. … She loved Silver Rail. This was her dream job. Meghan was compassionate and had a huge heart. She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs. She was an incredible sister, daughter, niece and granddaughter. … She was funny and opinionated and she lit up the room." Community members grieve at the site of a makeshift memorial in front of Silver Rail Elementary School. Mathieu Lewis-Rolland via Getty Images The shooter was identified as Griffin John II. He was a former student at the school who had received special ed services, according to Bend-La Pine School Superintendent Steven Cook. The names of the two other victims, who were 8 and 11 years old, have not been made public. A 7-year-old student and a teacher were hospitalized with critical injuries after the incident. The child, who has not been identified, is in "serious, but stable, condition," Krantz said. The wounded teacher was identified by the AP as Becky Drury, an educational assistant at Silver Rail Elementary. According to a Facebook post from her mother-in-law, Drury has already had surgery to repair significant damage to her left arm and will need more surgeries in the future. She also suffered injuries to her right hand, but none of her wounds are believed to be life-threatening. "The good news is she will be ok and we all get to keep that magnificent woman we love so much in our lives," the post read. Police declined to confirm the name of the bystander who killed John, but he had previously been identified by the Associated Press as Kyle Giamanco, a lifelong Bend resident and the father of two young daughters at the school. "He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support," Giamanco's mother, Kenda Freeman, said while reading a prepared statement to reporters outside her son's home near the school. "I don't think we can underestimate or underappreciate [his] courage," Krantz said Friday, referring to Giamanco's decision to intervene. "When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. And the quick thinking to … follow someone into the school is incredible, and undoubtedly saved people." Other than John's past association with the school, police did not share any information on the potential motive behind the shooting. "Everyone wants to know why, including us," Krantz said. "We may never get that full answer, but we want it." Krantz said John used a Maverick 88 12-gauge pump-action shotgun in the shooting. He declined to comment on where he acquired the gun. How the shooting unfolded Flowers are placed beside a sign at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Friday. AP Photo/Haven Daley Krantz provided new details about what happened in the chaotic few minutes from when John first opened fire outside the school to when he was killed. According to Krantz, John approached the school at approximately 12:58 p.m. on foot before throwing his gun over an exterior fence and climbing onto the school's property. A driver in a red pickup truck spotted John and "verbally confronted" him from inside their vehicle. John fired at least three rounds at the truck before heading inside. The driver, who was unhurt, quickly called 911 to alert police. John then walked around the outside of the school and fired multiple rounds into the glass panes of an exterior door to gain access to the school. He then turned left into a special education classroom and immediately began firing. In total, John fired as many as 15 rounds, Krantz said. Giamanco, who had seen John fire at the pickup truck, parked his car in the school parking lot, grabbed his pistol and began following John's path into the school. As he entered through the shot-out doors, Giamanco found a teacher involved in a physical altercation with John. He fired several rounds from his pistol, striking John multiple times. Officers arrived at the scene within three minutes of the first 911 call. "Seconds later, officers reported the suspect had been shot and killed, possibly by a bystander," police wrote in an incident report on Thursday. Officers then cleared the school, and all students and staff were transported to a nearby church for reunification with families and guardians. According to Krantz, John was carrying an additional 44 rounds of ammunition when he was killed. No other students other than the three who were killed and the one who was injured were in the classroom at the time, Krantz said. There was no School Resource Officer present at the school. 'They're babies' People leave a family reunification area following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Thursday. AP Photo/Joe Kline Witnesses described hearing gunshots and seeing police swarm the school. "I heard what I thought was gunshots," Erin Johnson, who was visiting her parents next door to the school, told Oregon Public Broadcasting on Thursday. "Then my neighbor began to scream shortly thereafter — her kids go to school there, at Silver Rail. Then I heard the police coming in." She added: "It's heartbreaking. I don't know any details right now about who was injured. But they're babies." Krista Johnson told OregonLive that she saw police swarm the school. "So many people stopping what they were doing," she said Thursday. "I knew that something had happened." Angela Nuchols told the Bend Source that she and her husband had dressed their 8-year-old daughter up for picture day before school, then raced to Silver Rail after hearing about the shooting. "It was crawling with police officers from all over the county," she said. "You've got guys in tactical gear, rifles. You're just scared to death wondering, is your child okay? You don't know." They were later reunited with their daughter. "It was like the worst three hours of our lives," Nuchols said. Thousands attended a vigil at Bend's Drake Park on Thursday night, many carrying candles, flowers and stuffed toys. "There is power and love in this park tonight," Kotek said at the vigil, according to OregonLive. "On behalf of everyone who lives in Oregon, I am so sorry for what you are experiencing today. No parent, no family, no community should have to have this kind of day." Free counseling is being offered to anyone in the community who may need help dealing the emotional weight of the tragedy. As of Friday afternoon, close to 200 people had already utilized those services, according to Deschutes County Health Services Director Mary Harris. The Bend Education Association, which represents 1,000 educators in the city, released a statement emphasizing the work that will be needed to ensure that every student and teacher affected by the shooting has the support that they need. "When violence happens in one of our schools, it reaches far beyond that building," the group's president, Sarah Barclay, wrote on social media. "It affects our families, our colleagues, and communities across our country. Every student and every person who works in our schools deserves to be safe." item.title: Body found in barrel at Lake Mead identified as 1980s shooting victim
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The remains of a man who was shot in the head and stuffed into a rusted barrel found on the shore of Lake Mead after the water level dropped were identified Thursday as an Arkansas man whose decades-old killing remains unsolved. Edward Lelburian Jackson was in his mid- to late 50s when he died, Clark County Coroner Melanie Rouse said. Authorities are looking for people to come forward to help solve Jackson's killing. There was no evidence directly linking the killing to organized crime in nearby Las Vegas despite longstanding speculation, although a connection hasn't been ruled out, police said. An expert on mob activity in the city said the case bears the "earmarks" of a mob hit and that questions still linger. The discovery sparked memories of Las Vegas' mob era Jackson was identified with the help of a bone sample sent for genealogy profiling, along with three angles of a composite face and clothing Jackson was wearing when he died, Rouse said. "We were able to confirm that the remains were in fact Edward Jackson," she said. The discovery of the barrel by boaters in May 2022 sparked memories of the city's mob era , which lasted from the 1940s to the mid-1980s. Organized crime helped build up Las Vegas, and a body stuffed in a barrel was known to signify a mob killing. Jackson, believed to be from Hot Springs, Arkansas, had a brief criminal history in the early 1980s in Salt Lake City, Utah, which included one charge of aggravated arson and conspiracy to commit fraud, said Robert Price, a Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department homicide lieutenant. Police said Jackson was married for a short time with no known children, CBS affiliate KLAS-TV reported . It's unclear why Jackson was in Las Vegas Price said there is nothing to tie the killing to organized crime. He added, however, that it hasn't been ruled out. Jackson's family told investigators that he liked to travel and detectives found records of him in California, where he lived with his wife in the early '70s. His family said they last saw him in Arkansas in the early '80s, and it is unclear why he was in Las Vegas. Homicide detectives will continue working to figure out what happened to him, said Price. "It's an unsolved case. It will never be closed until we solve it," Price said Thursday. "I would say that this is a piece of the puzzle and as we get more and more pieces, we'll be able to keep on digging deeper." Authorities had already said the man was shot, and they estimate he was killed in the early 1980s. Jackson had not been reported missing The man had been wearing a button-down short-sleeve shirt, light blue jeans, a silver wristwatch and blue-and-white tennis shoes. Price said the family didn't report him missing. "They knew that he had traveled the country, would show up when he showed up, just to say hi. But they didn't think anything other than that. They just figured he was out and about," he said. Researcher says case has all the "earmarks of a mob hit" Geoff Schumacher, vice president of research, collections and programs at The Mob Museum in Las Vegas, said there are still many questions about who Jackson was and what he was involved in that "earned him a trip in a barrel into the lake." Members of organized crime were involved in the Las Vegas casino industry from the 1940s to the mid-1980s, both behind the scenes and through shadow ownerships of casinos, Schumacher said. He said the case had all the "earmarks of a mob hit," mirroring another case from 1976 when Italian mobster John Roselli was killed and stuffed in a barrel and dumped into a bay outside of Miami Beach. Schumacher said he and Mob Museum staff will comb their records to try to help solve the case. "I think this story is not over," he said. Other bodies discovered as Lake Mead recedes Las Vegas historian Michael Green said whoever committed the crime probably thought the body would "never come near the surface." In the early 1980s, the lake levels were so high that the spillways flooded at Hoover Dam, he said. Now, Lake Mead is at a historic low due to years of overuse, longstanding drought and increasing temperatures. The water level of the 90-year-old reservoir has dropped, exposing areas that were previously underwater. In August, the water level dipped to 1,039.77 feet above sea level, according to the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation , well below the previous record low set in July 2022. Several other sets of remains were found at Lake Mead in 2022. Another set of skeletal remains was discovered that May, and they were identified as a drowning victim from 2002. Skeletal remains found in August were identified as a 52-year-old Las Vegas resident who disappeared in 1998. The remains of another drowning victim, Donald Smith, who was believed to have drowned in 1974 , were found in October 2022. Its receding waters are leaving behind the usual flotsam and jetsam of a lake heavily trafficked by weekend boaters — and even exposing a ship dating back to World War II. Lake Mead and the upstream Lake Powell are the largest human-made reservoirs in the U.S., part of a system that provides Colorado River water to people across the U.S. Southwest and Mexico. In 2022, Lake Mead's dropping level exposed Las Vegas' uppermost drinking water intake. That forced authorities to switch to a deeper intake to keep serving the city's 2.4 million residents. item.title: A teacher saved lives by tackling and fighting the Oregon shooter, police say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Deborah Bloom and Herbert Villarraga BEND, Oregon, Oct 16 (Reuters) - A 16-year-old boy who shot and killed a teacher and three children in an Oregon special-needs classroom was stopped by another teacher who tackled him and an armed father who fatally shot him, officials said on Friday. Their actions on Thursday saved other lives, the local police chief ‌told a press conference. A day into their investigation of the latest US school shooting, police released new details of the scene at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, ‌where three schoolchildren aged 5, 8 and 11 were killed along with 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert. A 7-year-old was wounded and listed in serious but stable condition, and another teacher suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, police said. TEACHER 'HELPED PREVENT MORE BLOODSHED,' POLICE SAY The unidentified ​teacher who stopped the shooter on Thursday threw her phone at him, tackled and fought him. A 36-year-old father of two students then rushed in with a legal .40-caliber pistol and fired at the suspect multiple times, killing him just before police arrived. This teacher, who was not injured, "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz, at times choking back emotion, told a press conference. "The teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that's true heroism," he said, without identifying her. Kenda Freeman told the New York Times that her son Kaylub Giamanco, whose two daughters attend the school, killed the shooter, according ‌to video posted by the New York Times of Freeman reading a brief ⁠statement. "He is not seeking recognition but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," Freeman said, adding that he asked for privacy and did not want to speak to the media. The shooting traumatized much of Bend, a city of ⁠about 100,000 people some 175 miles (280 km) southeast of Portland, including 9-year-old fourth-grader Kalani Journeigh and her classmates, who heard the gunshots from a nearby classroom. "All of us were screaming and we were all, like, really scared," Kalani told Reuters, adding that she feared, "We might die." "My heart was beating really fast and after the couple of gunshots that we heard, it just stopped and we never heard it again," she said. A friend of hers was ​going ​to get therapy, she said, because "that was really traumatizing to her." Officials identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, a ​16-year-old former special-needs student at the school who was armed with a shotgun. ‌He fired about 15 rounds in the classroom and had another 44 rounds on him, police said. Police were trying to determine what motivated the shooter and how he obtained a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun, Krantz said. "Everyone wants to know why, including us," the police chief said. "We may never get that full answer, but we want it." VICTIMS MOURNED Just before the shooting, the assailant was seen throwing his weapon over the school fence and then climbing after it onto school grounds. The driver of a truck passing by verbally confronted the boy, who opened fire on the vehicle. The assailant shot through locked glass doors and stormed a class of mixed-grade special-needs students. Police arrived within three minutes of the first call, and the shooter was already dead, Krantz said. People in Bend gathered near the school to mourn on ‌Friday morning, placing flowers and candles outside yellow-crime scene tape that cordoned off the scene. "Thank God for that father," ​Michael Zappa, 71, who lives just blocks from the school, said through tears. "He saved a lot of lives yesterday, and ​our prayers should go out for him because he has a lot on his mind ​today." The family of the slain teacher, Lambert, said working at Silver Rail was a "dream job" for her. "She always fought for the underdog and those with special ‌needs," the family said in a statement that was read aloud at Friday's ​news conference. Lambert's family also praised Giamanco and expressed gratitude ​to him. "We think he is a hero," the family said, according to the statement. US school shootings have become more frequent in recent years. Since the start of this year, 118 people have been wounded or killed in 149 incidents involving a gun fired or brandished in a school, or gunshots striking school property, according to the K-12 School Shooting Database, a ​nonprofit online tracker. A separate online database, the Gun Violence Archive, has recorded ‌371 mass shootings since January 2026, defining mass shootings as four or more people being struck by gunfire, not including the shooter. Three of those, including the Bend ​incident, occurred in public schools, the archive said. (Reporting by Deborah Bloom and Herbert Villarraga in Bend; Additional reporting by Jonathan Allen in New York and Steve Gorman in ​Los Angeles; Writing by Daniel Trotta; Editing by Paul Thomasch, Jonathan Spicer, Sergio Non and Cynthia Osterman) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/teacher-tackled-fought-oregon-school-221156030.html
